TipWhat is this?

For the next four weeks you will design and build a program that is bigger than anything you have made so far — and you will build it like real software makers do: plan first, save your progress with git, test it with pytest, ask people to try it, and explain your design. You can work alone or in a pair.

1. Choose your option

Option What you make Start from
(a) Grid game A game on a grid of squares: a maze, a dungeon, a puzzle, a farm. Characters are objects; enemies can use an algorithm to move. grid_game_template.py
(b) Generative art app An app that makes pictures from rules: fractals, patterns, tiles. Shapes are objects; your art can be saved and loaded again. art_app_template.py
(c) Data / AI app An app that answers questions about data, draws charts, or predicts things with a nearest-neighbor “AI”. data_app_template.py and data/games.csv

The templates are in the starter folder. They already run; the README.md there tells you how to copy the folder and make your first git commit.

2. The must-haves

Whatever you build, your finished project must have all of these. Check them off as you go.

Self-checkSelf-check: tick each box when it is true

3. Idea menu

Pick one, mix two, or invent your own. Small and finished beats huge and broken!

(a) Grid games & (b) Generative art & (c) Data / AI
Dungeon crawler: collect keys, open doors, a monster that hunts you with BFS & Fractal forest: trees with different depth, angle and season palettes; save your favorite settings & Game-night stats: survey your family’s favorite games, clean the data, chart it
Sokoban-style box pusher with levels in text files and an undo stack & Quilt maker: tiles of shape classes in a grid, mirror and rotate rules & Monster sorter: a nearest-neighbor AI guesses the type of a new monster from its features
Snake on a grid with a queue for the body & Flood-fill coloring book: click a region to fill it (recursion or BFS) & Weather or reading log: average, best week, a bar chart, a prediction
Farm or garden simulator: plants are objects that grow each tick & Spirograph studio: pattern classes, sliders by keys, a gallery saved as JSON & Story maker: a Markov text generator trained on your own stories

4. Milestones

Milestone & When & Done when…
M1 Pitch & end of week 9 & Your pitch page (section 5) is filled in and your teacher has said “go”. Your project folder exists and has its first commit.
M2 Design + core classes & week 10 & CRC cards and a class diagram are drawn. Your main classes exist in code, run without errors, and have the first 2 tests. At least 3 commits.
M3 Features + 5 tests + playtest & week 11, first half & The must-have features work, 5+ tests pass, and someone else has playtested it (feedback card filled in).
M4 README + polish & week 11, second half & You fixed the top bugs from the playtest, wrote the README, and have 8+ meaningful commits.
Showcase & week 12 & You show your project and explain one design decision.

TipCommit like a pro

Commit every time something small works: "Add Hero class", "Stop hero walking through walls", "Test that treasure adds 1 point". Messages like "stuff" or "final" do not count as meaningful.

6. Testing your project

Test the logic, not the drawing. Keep rules (moving, scoring, saving, sorting, predicting) in classes and functions that do not use turtle, and keep the turtle code in its own part. Ideas:

  • a wall blocks a move; collecting treasure adds a point;

  • your search or sort gives the right answer on a tiny example and an edge case (empty list, unreachable square);

  • saving and loading gives back the same data (use pytest’s tmp_path folder);

  • your classifier predicts the right label for an obvious example.

test_my_project.py in the starter folder has examples. Run your tests from Thonny’s Tools → Open system shell… with python3 -m pytest -q.

8. How your project is judged

Your teacher uses the same rubric. Before the showcase, check one box in each row: where do you think you are?

& Just starting & Getting there & Got it & Expert
Creativity & ☐ My idea is a copy of an example & ☐ I changed an example a bit & ☐ My project has my own idea and style & ☐ My project surprises people with something new
Working code & ☐ It crashes often & ☐ It runs, with some bugs & ☐ All must-have features work & ☐ It works well, even when people do unexpected things
Design / OOP & ☐ One class, or classes that do not help & ☐ 2 classes, but jobs are mixed up & ☐ Clear classes; inheritance or composition used well & ☐ I can show why my class design makes the code easier to change
Testing & ☐ Fewer than 3 tests & ☐ 3–4 tests, or tests that fail & ☐ 5+ passing tests of my logic & ☐ My tests include edge cases and caught a real bug
Git history & ☐ Fewer than 4 commits & ☐ 4–7 commits, or unclear messages & ☐ 8+ commits with clear messages & ☐ My log tells the story of my project step by step
Explaining design decisions & ☐ I can show what it does & ☐ I can explain how one part works & ☐ I can explain why I chose my design & ☐ I can compare my design with another way and explain the trade-off

9. Need more time, or want more?

Start from a starter template and keep it small: 2 classes, 3 features, 5 simple tests (one per method). Ask your teacher for a “feature card” with one small step at a time. It is fine to finish fewer features well. Add a second level or mode loaded from a file; write tests before the code (test-first); use BFS or recursion in a second place; add a settings dictionary saved as JSON; try k-nearest neighbors (3 vote) for option (c).

Show your nickname, never your real name, on screen. Photos or videos only if everyone agrees. Your project stays on our computers; we do not upload it anywhere.

Getting started (once, with your teacher)

  1. Copy this whole starter folder to your Documents folder and rename it, for example dragon-maze (no spaces is easiest in Terminal).
  2. Delete the templates you are not using. Rename yours, for example grid_game_template.py -> dragon_maze.py, and change the import line in test_my_project.py to match.
  3. Open a Terminal from Thonny: menu Tools > Open system shell... (this Terminal knows Thonny's Python, which has pytest installed). Type these lines, pressing Return after each one:
cd ~/Documents/dragon-maze
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Start my project from the starter kit"

That first commit is your first save point.

Git workflow cheat list

Do this loop many times: change a little -> run it -> test it -> commit.

I want to... Type this
go to my project folder cd ~/Documents/dragon-maze
see what changed git status
see the exact lines that changed git diff
choose a file for the next save point git add dragon_maze.py
choose every changed file git add .
make a save point git commit -m "Add a chaser that uses BFS"
see my save points git log --oneline
undo changes I have NOT committed yet git restore dragon_maze.py
run my tests (in Thonny's system shell) python3 -m pytest -q

Good commit messages say WHAT changed, in a few words, starting with a verb:

  • Good: Add Enemy class that inherits from Character
  • Good: Fix hero walking through the right-hand wall
  • Not helpful: stuff, changes, asdf, final final 2

Golden rules:

  • Commit at least once every session, and whenever something works.
  • Never commit secrets: no real names, passwords, addresses or photos.
  • Stay on one branch (the one git made for you). If git prints something that scares you, stop and ask - nothing is lost while it is committed.

README template (copy into a file called README.md in your project)

# <Project name>

<One sentence: what is it and who is it for?>

## How to run it
Open <file name>.py in Thonny and press Run.
Controls: <keys / clicks>

## What it does
- <feature 1>
- <feature 2>
- <feature 3>

## How it is built
- Classes: <ClassName> - <what it is for>; <ClassName> - <...>
- Inheritance or composition: <which class inherits from / has which>
- Data structure: <dict / stack / queue / grid> - <what it stores>
- Algorithm: <search / sort / recursion / BFS> - <where and why>
- Saved file: <file name> - <what is saved>

## Tests
Run `python3 -m pytest -q`. My tests check: <list>

## A design decision I am proud of
<What did you choose, what else could you have done, and why is your way better?>

## Credits
<Ideas, sounds, pictures, code examples you used and who made them>

What is .gitignore?

A hidden file in this folder that lists files git should never save, such as Python's __pycache__ folder. You do not need to change it.

art_app_template.py

"""My Art App - starter template for project option (b).

This already works: press Run, click to add shapes, press S to save your
picture and L to load it again. Your job is to make it YOURS: new shape
classes, a recursive pattern, your own palette. Look for the TODO comments.

Before you start, rename this file to a name nobody else uses,
for example spiral_studio.py, and change the import in test_my_project.py.
"""

import json
import random
import turtle
from pathlib import Path

SAVE_FILE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "my_art.json"

# Okabe-Ito color-blind-safe palette
PALETTE = ["#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442",
           "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#000000"]


class Shape:
    """Base class: every shape has a kind, a position, a size and a color."""

    kind = "dot"

    def __init__(self, x, y, size, color):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.size = size
        self.color = color

    def draw(self, pen):
        pen.goto(self.x, self.y)
        pen.dot(self.size, self.color)

    def to_dict(self):
        """Turn the shape into a dictionary so json can save it."""
        return {"kind": self.kind, "x": self.x, "y": self.y,
                "size": self.size, "color": self.color}


class Square(Shape):
    """A Square IS a Shape (inheritance). It only changes how it draws."""

    kind = "square"

    def draw(self, pen):
        pen.goto(self.x - self.size / 2, self.y - self.size / 2)
        pen.color(self.color)
        pen.pendown()
        pen.begin_fill()
        for _ in range(4):
            pen.forward(self.size)
            pen.left(90)
        pen.end_fill()
        pen.penup()


# TODO: add your own shape class, e.g. class Star(Shape).
# TODO (algorithm): add a RECURSIVE shape, e.g. a fractal tree or a spiral:
#     def draw(self, pen): ... calls a helper that calls itself with a
#     smaller size, and STOPS at a base case (size < 5).

SHAPE_CLASSES = {"dot": Shape, "square": Square}  # TODO: add your classes here


def shape_from_dict(data):
    """The opposite of to_dict: build the right kind of shape again."""
    shape_class = SHAPE_CLASSES[data["kind"]]
    return shape_class(data["x"], data["y"], data["size"], data["color"])


class Gallery:
    """A Gallery HAS a list of shapes (composition)."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.shapes = []

    def add(self, shape):
        self.shapes.append(shape)

    def draw_all(self, pen):
        pen.clear()
        for shape in self.shapes:
            shape.draw(pen)  # each shape draws itself its own way

    def save(self, filename):
        with open(filename, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
            data = [shape.to_dict() for shape in self.shapes]
            json.dump(data, file, indent=1)

    def load(self, filename):
        """Replace the shapes with the ones in the file (if it exists)."""
        if not Path(filename).exists():
            return False
        with open(filename, encoding="utf-8") as file:
            self.shapes = [shape_from_dict(data) for data in json.load(file)]
        return True


def main():
    gallery = Gallery()
    pen = turtle.Turtle()
    pen.hideturtle()
    pen.penup()
    screen = turtle.Screen()
    screen.title("My Art App - click to add, S to save, L to load")
    screen.tracer(0)

    def add_shape(x, y):
        shape_class = random.choice(list(SHAPE_CLASSES.values()))
        size = random.randint(10, 60)
        gallery.add(shape_class(x, y, size, random.choice(PALETTE)))
        gallery.draw_all(pen)
        screen.update()

    def save():
        gallery.save(SAVE_FILE)

    def load():
        gallery.load(SAVE_FILE)
        gallery.draw_all(pen)
        screen.update()

    screen.onclick(add_shape)
    screen.onkey(save, "s")
    screen.onkey(load, "l")
    screen.listen()
    add_shape(0, 0)  # start with one shape so the window is not empty


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
    turtle.done()

data_app_template.py

"""My Data / AI App - starter template for project option (c).

This already works: press Run to load data/games.csv (made-up games, no
personal data), print a summary and draw a bar chart. Your job is to make
it YOURS: your own data, more questions, and a simple AI that predicts.
Look for the TODO comments.

Before you start, rename this file to a name nobody else uses,
for example game_guesser.py, and change the import in test_my_project.py.
"""

import csv
import turtle
from pathlib import Path

DATA_FILE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "data" / "games.csv"
NUMBER_COLUMNS = ["players", "minutes", "action", "puzzle", "rating"]
BAR_COLORS = ["#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73",
               "#CC79A7", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00"]


def clean_row(row):
    """Tidy one row: strip spaces, lower-case words, turn numbers into ints.
    Returns None for an empty row. A blank number becomes None."""
    row = {key: (value or "").strip() for key, value in row.items()}
    if not row["name"]:
        return None
    row["genre"] = row["genre"].lower()
    for column in NUMBER_COLUMNS:
        row[column] = int(row[column]) if row[column].isdigit() else None
    return row


class DataSet:
    """A DataSet HAS a list of rows (each row is a dictionary)."""

    def __init__(self, rows):
        self.rows = rows

    def count_by(self, column):
        """How many rows have each value? e.g. {"action": 5, "puzzle": 5}"""
        counts = {}
        for row in self.rows:
            counts[row[column]] = counts.get(row[column], 0) + 1
        return counts

    def average(self, column):
        """Average of a number column, ignoring blanks (None)."""
        values = [row[column] for row in self.rows if row[column] is not None]
        if not values:
            return 0
        return sum(values) / len(values)

    def top(self, column, n=3):
        """The n rows with the biggest value in column (a sort with key=)."""
        rows = [row for row in self.rows if row[column] is not None]
        return sorted(rows, key=lambda row: row[column], reverse=True)[:n]


def load_dataset(filename):
    with open(filename, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        rows = [clean_row(row) for row in csv.DictReader(file)]
    return DataSet([row for row in rows if row is not None])


def distance(a, b, features):
    """How different are two rows? Add up the gaps between their features."""
    return sum(abs(a[f] - b[f]) for f in features)


# TODO (AI): write nearest_neighbor(dataset, mystery, features) that finds
# the row with the SMALLEST distance to the mystery game and returns its
# genre. Try mystery = {"action": 5, "puzzle": 1}. Then test it!
# TODO (stretch): k-nearest neighbors - let the 3 closest rows vote.


def draw_bar_chart(counts, title):
    """Bars with the label AND the number written on them (not color only)."""
    pen = turtle.Turtle()
    pen.hideturtle()
    pen.penup()
    width, gap, scale = 60, 20, 40
    x = -(len(counts) * (width + gap)) / 2
    pen.goto(0, 180)
    pen.write(title, align="center", font=("Arial", 16, "bold"))
    for i, (label, count) in enumerate(sorted(counts.items())):
        pen.goto(x, -150)
        pen.color("black", BAR_COLORS[i % len(BAR_COLORS)])
        pen.pendown()
        pen.begin_fill()
        for side in [width, count * scale, width, count * scale]:
            pen.forward(side)
            pen.left(90)
        pen.end_fill()
        pen.penup()
        pen.goto(x + width / 2, -175)
        pen.write(label, align="center", font=("Arial", 12, "normal"))
        pen.goto(x + width / 2, -145 + count * scale)
        pen.write(str(count), align="center", font=("Arial", 12, "bold"))
        x += width + gap
    turtle.update()


def main():
    data = load_dataset(DATA_FILE)
    print(f"Loaded {len(data.rows)} games.")
    print("Average rating:", round(data.average("rating"), 1))
    for row in data.top("rating"):
        print(f"  {row['name']}: {row['rating']}")
    turtle.tracer(0)
    draw_bar_chart(data.count_by("genre"), "Games per genre")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
    turtle.done()

grid_game_template.py

"""My Grid Game - starter template for project option (a).

This already works: press Run and move the hero (H) with the arrow keys.
Your job is to turn it into YOUR game. Look for the TODO comments.

Before you start, rename this file to a name nobody else uses,
for example dragon_maze.py, and change the import in test_my_project.py.
"""

import turtle

CELL = 30  # size of one square in pixels

# A level is just text: # = wall, . = floor, H = hero, * = treasure.
# TODO: design your own level here (or load it from a file, see save_level).
LEVEL = """
##########
#H.....*.#
#.####...#
#....#.#.#
#.*..#.#.#
######...#
#*.......#
##########
"""


class Grid:
    """A 2D grid of one-letter strings: grid.cells[row][col]."""

    def __init__(self, text):
        lines = [line for line in text.strip().splitlines() if line]
        self.rows = len(lines)
        self.cols = max(len(line) for line in lines)
        # ljust pads short rows with walls so every row is the same length
        self.cells = [list(line.ljust(self.cols, "#")) for line in lines]

    def in_bounds(self, row, col):
        return 0 <= row < self.rows and 0 <= col < self.cols

    def get(self, row, col):
        return self.cells[row][col]

    def set(self, row, col, value):
        self.cells[row][col] = value

    def find(self, letter):
        """Return (row, col) of the first square holding letter, or None."""
        for row in range(self.rows):
            for col in range(self.cols):
                if self.cells[row][col] == letter:
                    return (row, col)
        return None

    def count(self, letter):
        return sum(row.count(letter) for row in self.cells)

    def is_open(self, row, col):
        return self.in_bounds(row, col) and self.cells[row][col] != "#"

    def neighbors(self, row, col):
        """Open squares next to (row, col): up, down, left, right."""
        result = []
        for d_row, d_col in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]:
            if self.is_open(row + d_row, col + d_col):
                result.append((row + d_row, col + d_col))
        return result

    def to_text(self):
        return "\n".join("".join(row) for row in self.cells)

    # TODO (saved file): add save_level(filename) and a load_level(filename)
    # function, so your levels live in .txt files next to this program.


class Hero:
    """The player. TODO: make a base class (for example Character) and let
    Hero AND a new Enemy class inherit from it (or use composition)."""

    def __init__(self, row, col):
        self.row = row
        self.col = col
        self.treasure = 0

    def move(self, grid, d_row, d_col):
        """Step one square unless a wall is in the way. True if moved."""
        new_row, new_col = self.row + d_row, self.col + d_col
        if not grid.is_open(new_row, new_col):
            return False
        grid.set(self.row, self.col, ".")
        self.row, self.col = new_row, new_col
        if grid.get(new_row, new_col) == "*":
            self.treasure += 1
        grid.set(new_row, new_col, "H")
        return True


# TODO (algorithm): add breadth-first search, flood fill or a recursive
# function. Idea: an enemy that uses BFS (with collections.deque) to chase H.


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drawing
# Shapes AND letters, so the game never depends on color alone.
COLORS = {"#": "#0072B2", "*": "#E69F00", "H": "#009E73"}


def draw(pen, grid, hero):
    pen.clear()
    left = -grid.cols * CELL / 2
    top = grid.rows * CELL / 2
    for row in range(grid.rows):
        for col in range(grid.cols):
            letter = grid.get(row, col)
            x = left + col * CELL
            y = top - row * CELL
            if letter in COLORS:
                pen.goto(x, y)
                pen.color("black", COLORS[letter])
                pen.begin_fill()
                for _ in range(4):
                    pen.forward(CELL)
                    pen.right(90)
                pen.end_fill()
            if letter in "H*":
                pen.goto(x + CELL / 2, y - CELL + 6)
                pen.write(letter, align="center", font=("Arial", 14, "bold"))
    pen.goto(0, top + 10)
    pen.write(f"Treasure: {hero.treasure}", align="center",
              font=("Arial", 14, "bold"))
    turtle.update()


def main():
    grid = Grid(LEVEL)
    row, col = grid.find("H")
    hero = Hero(row, col)
    pen = turtle.Turtle()
    pen.hideturtle()
    pen.penup()

    def go(d_row, d_col):
        hero.move(grid, d_row, d_col)
        draw(pen, grid, hero)

    screen = turtle.Screen()
    screen.title("My Grid Game")
    screen.tracer(0)
    screen.onkey(lambda: go(-1, 0), "Up")
    screen.onkey(lambda: go(1, 0), "Down")
    screen.onkey(lambda: go(0, -1), "Left")
    screen.onkey(lambda: go(0, 1), "Right")
    screen.listen()
    draw(pen, grid, hero)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
    turtle.done()

test_my_project.py

"""Example tests for the three starter templates.

1. Keep the section for the option you chose and delete the other two.
2. When you rename your program, change the import line to match.
3. Add your OWN tests until you have at least 5 (the project needs 5+).
   A good test: set something up, do ONE thing, then assert what you expect.

Run them in Terminal, from your project folder:   python3 -m pytest -q
"""

import sys
from pathlib import Path

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(HERE))  # so Python finds the programs in this folder

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- option (a)
import grid_game_template as game  # noqa: E402  (change to your file name)

TINY = """
#####
#H.*#
#####
"""


def test_grid_reads_the_level():
    grid = game.Grid(TINY)
    assert (grid.rows, grid.cols) == (3, 5)
    assert grid.find("H") == (1, 1)
    assert grid.count("*") == 1


def test_hero_cannot_walk_through_walls():
    grid = game.Grid(TINY)
    hero = game.Hero(1, 1)
    assert hero.move(grid, -1, 0) is False, "There is a wall above the hero."
    assert (hero.row, hero.col) == (1, 1)


def test_hero_collects_treasure():
    grid = game.Grid(TINY)
    hero = game.Hero(1, 1)
    hero.move(grid, 0, 1)
    hero.move(grid, 0, 1)
    assert hero.treasure == 1 and grid.count("*") == 0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- option (b)
import art_app_template as art  # noqa: E402


def test_gallery_save_and_load_round_trip(tmp_path):
    gallery = art.Gallery()
    gallery.add(art.Square(10, 20, 30, "#0072B2"))
    gallery.add(art.Shape(-5, 0, 12, "#E69F00"))
    gallery.save(tmp_path / "art.json")
    copy = art.Gallery()
    assert copy.load(tmp_path / "art.json")
    saved = [s.to_dict() for s in gallery.shapes]
    assert [s.to_dict() for s in copy.shapes] == saved
    assert isinstance(copy.shapes[0], art.Square), \
        "Loading should rebuild the right class."

import data_app_template as data_app  # noqa: E402


def test_cleaning_skips_empty_rows_and_tidies_text():
    data = data_app.load_dataset(data_app.DATA_FILE)
    assert len(data.rows) == 13, "The empty row should be skipped."
    assert data.count_by("genre")["action"] == 5, \
        "' Action ' should be cleaned to 'action'."


def test_average_ignores_blanks():
    data = data_app.DataSet([{"rating": 4}, {"rating": None}, {"rating": 2}])
    assert data.average("rating") == 3
